title: Algebraic Expressions
tagline: Year 2 — Identities, factorisation and evaluating expressions quickly

introduction.overview: An algebraic expression combines numbers and letters with operations. The most useful tools in aptitude tests are the standard identities, such as (a + b)² and a² − b², which let you simplify, factorise and evaluate expressions without long arithmetic. A little algebra often turns a heavy calculation into a one-line answer.
introduction.placementRelevance: Algebraic identities are commonly used in company aptitude rounds for simplification questions and for finding values like a² + b² when a + b and ab are known.
introduction.realWorldContext: Simplifying formulas in engineering, checking expressions in code and reducing calculation effort by factoring all use the same identities.

learningObjectives: Use the identities (a ± b)², a² − b², (a ± b)³ and a³ ± b³
Evaluate expressions such as a² + b² from a + b and ab
Factorise quadratic expressions and simple polynomials
Use identities to compute squares and products quickly

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Like terms can be added; (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. A negative sign outside a bracket changes all signs inside.

coreDefinitions: Expression: a combination of constants, variables and operations, with no equals sign.
Term: each part separated by + or −. Factor: a quantity that divides an expression exactly.
Identity: an equation true for all values of the variables.
Factorisation: writing an expression as a product of simpler expressions.
Coefficient: the number multiplying a variable.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Identities are shortcuts that hold for every number. Instead of computing 102² by long multiplication, write (100 + 2)² = 10000 + 400 + 4. Algebra is just organised arithmetic.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Look for patterns: two squares with a minus (difference of squares), a perfect square trinomial, or a sum/difference that equals something known. Then apply the matching identity.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Square identities
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²;  (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Difference of squares
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Factor a difference of two squares.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Cube identities
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³;  a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²);  a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)

mainNarrative: The two identities to memorise first are (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). With them, 102² = (100 + 2)² = 10,404, and 1002² − 998² = (1002 − 998)(1002 + 998) = 4 × 2000 = 8,000.
To find a² + b² from a + b = 7 and ab = 10, use (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², so a² + b² = 49 − 20 = 29. Similarly a² + b² = (a − b)² + 2ab.
For reciprocal pairs: if x + 1/x = 3, then x² + 1/x² = 3² − 2 = 7 and x³ + 1/x³ = 3³ − 3 × 3 = 18.
To factorise a quadratic x² + px + q, find two numbers whose sum is p and product is q. x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5).
For sums and differences of cubes, a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²). For 5³ + 3³ = 125 + 27 = 152, and (5 + 3)(25 − 15 + 9) = 8 × 19 = 152.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why identities speed up arithmetic
deepDiveAspects.content: Large squares become sums of small numbers. 99² = (100 − 1)² = 10,000 − 200 + 1 = 9,801.

deepDiveAspects.title: Checking by substitution
deepDiveAspects.content: To verify a factorisation, put a simple value for x. If x = 1 gives different values on both sides, the factorisation is wrong.

solvedExamples.title: a² + b² from a + b and ab
solvedExamples.question: If a + b = 7 and ab = 10, find a² + b².
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The two unknowns need not be found individually.

solvedExamples.title: Reciprocal pair
solvedExamples.question: If x + 1/x = 3, find x² + 1/x² and x³ + 1/x³.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Square and cube the given sum.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The cross terms are known from the given sum.

shortcutMethods.title: Pattern spotting

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Expand and multiply out in full.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Spot (a ± b)², a² − b² or a known sum and product, then substitute into the identity.

rulesForApplication: Check by substituting a small number.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Test options with a quick substitution; wrong options usually fail at a small value.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Identities also appear inside quadratic equation questions.
